title: Songlin Yang (@SonglinYang4)
clean_title: 27x faster Attention Residuals with Block AttnRes
summary:
27x faster Attention Residuals!!! 🚀
We implemented Block AttnRes as a pip-installable package.
!pip install flash-attn-res
No annoying kernel nonsense.
No compile/autograd plumbing.
Call it like a regular PyTorch op.
It just works.
Methodology:
🔹 fused triton kernels
🔹 batched attention over residual blocks
🔹 online-softmax merge
🔹 flash attention-style split-KV reduction
Thanks @LLMenjoyer and @cartesia for the support and guidance✌️
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HHZ2MWlXkAAxBJi.jpg
Quoting @Kimi_Moonshot
Introducing 𝑨𝒕𝒕𝒆𝒏𝒕𝒊𝒐𝒏 𝑹𝒆𝒔𝒊𝒅𝒖𝒂𝒍𝒔: Rethinking depth-wise aggregation.
Residual connections have long relied on fixed, uniform accumulation. Inspired by the duality of time and depth, we introduce Attention Residuals, replacing standard depth-wise recurrence with learned, input-dependent attention over preceding layers.
🔹 Enables networks to selectively retrieve past representations, naturally mitigating dilution and hidden-state growth.
🔹 Introduces Block AttnRes, partitioning layers into compressed blocks to make cross-layer attention practical at scale.
🔹 Serves as an efficient drop-in replacement, demonstrating a 1.25x compute advantage with negligible (<2%) inference latency overhead.
🔹 Validated on the Kimi Linear architecture (48B total, 3B activated parameters), delivering consistent downstream performance gains.
🔗Full report:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HDgCpkHb0AA0a7_.jpg
clean_summary:
A new implementation called Block AttnRes achieves 27 times faster attention residuals. It is available as a pip-installable package that works like a regular PyTorch operation without the need for kernel nonsense or compile/autograd plumbing. The method uses fused Triton kernels, batched attention over residual blocks, online-softmax merge, and split-KV reduction similar to flash attention.

Attention Residuals replace standard depth-wise recurrence with learned, input-dependent attention over previous layers, enabling networks to selectively retrieve past representations. This approach mitigates issues like dilution and hidden-state growth. The Block AttnRes partitions layers into compressed blocks, making cross-layer attention practical at scale, and offers a 1.25x compute advantage with minimal inference latency overhead. Validated on a large architecture with 48B total parameters, it delivers consistent performance gains while being easy to integrate as a drop-in replacement.

summary:
Introducing SubQ - a major breakthrough in LLM intelligence.
It is the first model built on a fully sub-quadratic sparse-attention architecture (SSA),
And the first frontier model with a 12 million token context window which is:
- 52x faster than FlashAttention at 1MM tokens
- Less than 5% the cost of Opus
Transformer-based LLMs waste compute by processing every possible relationship between words (standard attention).
Only a small fraction actually matter.
@subquadratic finds and focuses only on the ones that do.
That's nearly 1,000x less compute and a new way for LLMs to scale.

clean_summary:
Introducing SubQ, a major breakthrough in LLM intelligence. It is the first model built on a fully sub-quadratic sparse-attention architecture and features a 12 million token context window. This design makes it 52 times faster than FlashAttention at 1 million tokens and costs less than 5% of Opus.

Standard transformer-based LLMs waste compute by processing all possible relationships between words, but only a small fraction are actually important. SubQ identifies and focuses only on the relationships that matter, reducing compute by nearly 1,000 times and offering a new way for LLMs to scale.

"Demystifying Manifold Constraints in LLM Pre-training"
LLM pre-training depends on a stack of heuristic tricks, eg. normalization layers, weight decay, and optimizer tuning.
This paper suggests that by constraining weight matrices to geometric manifolds like spectral or Frobenius spheres reduces most of these heuristics.
They introduced this optimizer called MACRO, which is a single-loop Riemannian method with provable convergence that keeps weights on-manifold every step.
Manifold constraints bound activation scales, replacing learnable RMSNorm. Muon diverges without it but MACRO doesn't. They also lock the relative learning rate from step one, replacing weight decay entirely as ablations show it has zero effect.

This sprint, I built a Lean4-to-TileLang Tensor Program Superoptimizer. With this, I now have a formal infrastructure where I (or my agents) can define neural network architectures in Lean4, and automatically get:

title: Songlin Yang (@SonglinYang4)
clean_title: OpenAI achieves breakthrough on Erdős' Planar Unit Distance problem
summary:
A breakthrough by OpenAI in a very famous Combinatorics problem, the Planar Unit Distance problem by Erdos 1946.
The problem is amazing because it can be described to a first-grader: Find a way to place n points on the plane to maximize the number of pairs that have distance exactly 1.
For example, if you have n=4 points on a square (of side-length 1) you have 4 pairs of distance 1. The diagonals have length sqrt(2) so don't count.
But you can squeeze one diagonal and create a point-set with n=4 points and 5 pairs of distance 1. And you can't get more than 5 pairs from n=4 points, so we are done with n=4 points.
Now, if you place n points on a line, you have n-1 pairs of distance 1. In general, all known constructions of n points had a number of pairs scaling essentially linearly: n^{1+something vanishing}
It seems that the model found a way to
place n points on the plane so that their unit distances scale super-linearly: like n^{1+delta} for some *constant* delta. Delta was not explicitly specified apparently, but a forthcoming refinement by Will Sawin shows delta=0.014 works, according to the announcement.
This is incredible progress for mathematics, since this is (unlike previous Erdos problems solved by AI) a major breakthrough, in one of the most studied problems in combinatorial geometry. If you're in mathematics research now, you feel the AGI.
Lijie Chen said it honestly in the video:
"It's very hard to sleep, man"
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HI0viqkaIAA7iKp.jpg
clean_summary: OpenAI has made a major breakthrough on the famous Planar Unit Distance problem posed by Erdős in 1946. The problem asks how to place n points on a plane to maximize the number of pairs exactly one unit apart, with known constructions scaling roughly linearly with n. The new model appears to place n points so that the number of unit-distance pairs grows super-linearly, approximately as n^{1+delta} with delta around 0.014, according to upcoming refinements. This progress is significant because it addresses a long-standing, well-studied problem in combinatorial geometry, marking a notable achievement in mathematical research and AI's capabilities.

title: Songlin Yang (@SonglinYang4)
clean_title: A new attention variant based on context-free value vectors with memory savings
summary:
In our new paper, we naturally derive a new attention variant based on the surprising finding that deep layers benefit the most from learning a context-free value vectors, without the input from the residual stream.
The attention variant: since the value vector does not depend on the context, it can be directly learned as sparse model parameter, and stored in a table of value vectors for the current layer.
The idea of having a value vector table is not new. Nanochat, for example, has it. But it was always learned as an extra group of weights to add to the existing value vector. With the insight that the deep layer **only** need a context-free vector, we can rewrite attention completely, by making the table the only source of value vectors.
On two model sizes we see that it significantly outperforms the standard attention baseline on both validation loss and benchmark scores, and slightly surpasses the strictly more expressive nanochat variant.
Besides the boost in performance, some very interesting consequences emerge in terms of memory:
- We do not need V cache anymore for the deep layers, and at long context it saves memory.
- Because we only need the token IDs for fetching value vectors, we can offload the table entirely, and just prefetch the relevant entries when previous layers are busy computing.
Me and @YuchenL52766559 are fascinated by this attention architecture's unique properties, and are doing experiments on bigger scales with it.
Paper:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJiHKVUbkAALgTr.jpg
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJiHRSRa4AAaERS.png
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJiHUXlbYAA6AcL.jpg
clean_summary:
A new attention variant is derived from the finding that deep layers benefit most from learning a context-free value vector, which can be stored in a table of value vectors for the current layer. Unlike previous methods like Nanochat, where the value table was learned as an extra set of weights, this approach makes the table the sole source of value vectors, simplifying the attention mechanism.

Experiments on two model sizes show this variant significantly outperforms the standard attention baseline in validation loss and benchmark scores, and slightly surpasses the more expressive Nanochat variant. Additionally, it eliminates the need for V cache in deep layers, saving memory at long contexts, and allows offloading the value table entirely, with prefetching of relevant entries. The researchers are exploring this architecture further on larger scales.

title: Songlin Yang (@SonglinYang4)
summary:
Some of the more puzzling unpublished observations from our paper: deep attention layers hate the residual stream of V and love it for QK, but if it has to make a choice, it will satisfy V over QK.
Translated to finding: if we learn coefficients for residual stream xi and the initial token embedding x0 as two input streams to deep attention layers, the model will give the coefficient for x0 a much larger magnitude. This will mean dominating the input with context-free token information.
However, if we learn the coefficients for both at a more fine-grained level for Q, K, and V, the coefficients for x0 is near 0 for both QK, but huge for V.
This reveals two surprises. (1) QK needs context information and little original token information. And K does not need the same information as V does (despite some models tying them). (2) Between the two opposite needs, the model is clearly in favor of what benefits V, so V is deemed more important to the optimization goal.
These are just the tip of an iceberg, and transformers surely moves in mysterious ways. We will therefore embark on the second part of this journey and, for our next set of experiments, involve this lady (iykyk)...

title: Songlin Yang (@SonglinYang4)
clean_title: Deep transformer layers: value vectors rely on token identity, queries and keys seek context
summary:
A quick follow up to our paper. We found that in the deep layers of a transformer, the value vectors don't need the residual stream. The token's own identity is enough to produce them. The question we kept coming back to was whether the same holds for the queries and keys, or only the value.
So we ran a small experiment. We took an attention residual model and let q, k, and v each learn, on their own and per layer, which earlier layer to read from. Then we just looked at what each one picked.
They split. In the deep layers the value keeps reading the original token, while the query and key move on to the recent layers, the part of the stream that actually carries context. Which makes sense. q and k decide what attends to what, so they need the context. The value is just the content that gets moved, and by then the token alone does the job. It is also why we only swap out the value and leave q and k alone.
One more thing we noticed but aren't sure about yet. When the value does reach back to earlier layers, it mostly skips the attention outputs and reads from the MLP outputs instead. The MLP works on each token on its own, while attention is where tokens get mixed together, so it fits the same picture. The value goes for what a token carries by itself and stays away from where the context comes in. Still early, but we thought it was a fun one.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJ8hIDjXUAEQkbS.png
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJ8hLHfXUAAxnUR.jpg
clean_summary: A follow-up to a recent paper reveals that in deep transformer layers, the value vectors do not need the residual stream; the token's own identity suffices to produce them. An experiment showed that in the deep layers, value vectors continue to read from the original token, while queries and keys move on to later layers that carry contextual information. This makes sense because queries and keys determine what attends to what, requiring context, whereas values simply carry content. Additionally, when values revisit earlier layers, they tend to skip attention outputs and read from the MLP outputs, which process tokens individually. This suggests that values focus on the token's intrinsic content, separate from the context integration happening through attention.

title: Songlin Yang (@SonglinYang4)
clean_title: Compositional Muon: An optimizer respecting transformer circuit structure
summary:
Introducing Compositional Muon, an optimizer that extends Muon from individual matrices to composed transformer circuits.
Modern optimizers usually draw trust regions around individual parameters. But in attention, the loss often sees compositions like QK^T and OV. Updating each factor independently can therefore control the wrong object.
Compositional Muon closes this gap by deriving partner-whitened update rules. Each factor’s update is shaped by the spectral geometry of the matrix it is composed with, producing more stable composed updates and better effective learning-rate allocation across heads and layers.
For QK, this gives a head-local half-split rule. For OV, the circuit geometry selects a hybrid rule: (V) is optimized per-head, while (W_O) is optimized as the single matrix that aggregates all heads back into the residual stream.
CM improves over Muon at 340M and 1B scale, transfers to the modded-nanoGPT optimization benchmark, and can be approximated cheaply as partner-rescaled Muon via the isotropic rule.
The broader point is optimizer-architecture co-design: better optimizers should not only ask how to update a parameter, but what composed circuit that parameter participates in. CM is one step toward optimizers that respect the functional structure the loss actually sees.
Quoting @tilderesearch
clean_summary:
Introducing Compositional Muon, an optimizer that extends Muon from updating individual matrices to handling entire transformer circuits. While most optimizers focus on parameters in isolation, this method considers the spectral geometry of matrix compositions like QK^T and OV, leading to more stable updates and better learning-rate allocation across heads and layers.

It derives partner-whitened update rules that adapt to the circuit's structure, such as a head-local half-split rule for QK and a hybrid rule for OV, optimizing V per head and W_O as a single matrix. CM outperforms Muon at 340M and 1B scales, transfers to nanoGPT benchmarks, and can be approximated as partner-rescaled Muon. The broader goal is optimizer-architecture co-design, where optimizers understand the functional structure of the circuits they update, moving toward more structure-aware optimization.

title: Songlin Yang (@SonglinYang4)
clean_title: Insights on optimizer sensitivity, hyper-parameter tuning, and LLM training strategies
summary:
I spent quite a bit of time last year comparing Shampoo/SOAP-like optimizers with Muon.
My main takeaway was that, beyond LR and weight decay, they are extremely sensitive to the various epsilon choices.
Two experiments stuck with me:
- A tiny change to eps was enough to flip the ranking between SOAP-like and Muon.
- Different nondeterministic training runs could also flip the ranking between Shampoo/SOAP-like and Muon.
What still puzzles me is that, from many theoretical angles, Muon looks like a nerfed version of Shampoo/SOAP. Yet in language modeling, Shampoo/SOAP-like methods — despite carrying extra optimizer states and more hyperparameters — still struggle to clearly beat Muon on validation loss.
My guess is that this is tied to the structure of LLMs and the LM task itself. On other tasks, Shampoo/SOAP-like methods may show a much cleaner advantage over Muon.
Quoting @_arohan_
Hyper-parameter tuning works really well!
Since Keller asked very nicely - I took it as a challenge to find a minimal edit distance from his config to a working config with no further code modifications, which means vanilla Meta's distributed_shampoo PyTorch package as is which won the AlgoPerf competition.
Biggest alpha here was tuning hyper-parameters apart from enabling pseudo inverse which was critical as this speed run problem produces rank deficient matrices (see those nice viz), and thanks to great help from Anna!
Hypers: lr=0.01, wd=0.1, beta2=0.9, eps=1e-15, freq=1 🙃
No Nesterov momentum was used. Oops.
All that is no longer needed - those modifications just was giving us identical training curves for same step targets because that's how math works, now the curves look different, but arrive at these end of train validation targets.
- first completed segment: step:3375/3375 val_loss:3.27656
- second completed segment: step:3375/3375 val_loss:3.27675
[1]
Next steps for anyone looking for a late night hobby:
* I would probably fuse lot of these things, make kernels
* Try it on new baselines, harder tasks: increase batch size or change architecture.
* Tune frequency, change eigh to ortho items etc.

clean_summary:
Last year, comparing Shampoo/SOAP-like optimizers with Muon revealed they are highly sensitive to epsilon choices, with small changes flipping their rankings and different runs producing variability. Despite Muon appearing as a simplified version of Shampoo/SOAP from a theoretical perspective, Shampoo/SOAP-like methods still struggle to outperform Muon on language modeling validation loss, possibly due to the structure of LLMs and their tasks.

A detailed example shows hyper-parameter tuning, especially epsilon and learning rate, can significantly impact training outcomes. Tuning hyperparameters like lr=0.01, wd=0.1, beta2=0.9, and eps=1e-15, along with kernel modifications, led to identical training curves and validation results, demonstrating the importance of careful hyper-parameter selection. Future steps include fusing optimizer techniques, experimenting on harder tasks, and adjusting parameters like frequency and eigen-decomposition methods to improve performance.

title: Songlin Yang (@SonglinYang4)
clean_title: ReplaySSM caches recent inputs to reduce memory traffic in hybrid models
summary:
Why do we store the SSM state at all?
More and more models are hybrids (Nemotron-3, Qwen3.5), so SSM decode speed matters.
We only write it back every step so the next step can read it.
ReplaySSM caches the recent inputs instead and rebuilds the state on the fly.
Same outputs, half the memory traffic
→ ~2x on spec decode at large batch sizes, which barely even helped SSMs before
→ up to 1.43x standard decode on large hybrids (up to Nemotron-Ultra-550B)
Work with @tri_dao
Blog + Code👇
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HK2-YW6WgAA5uvr.jpg
clean_summary: Why do we store the SSM state at all? As models become hybrids like Nemotron-3 and Qwen3.5, decode speed for SSM matters. Instead of writing back the state every step, ReplaySSM caches recent inputs and rebuilds the state on the fly, resulting in the same outputs but half the memory traffic. This approach achieves approximately twice the decode speed on large batch sizes and up to 1.43 times the standard decode speed on large hybrids like Nemotron-Ultra-550B. Work done with @tri_dao.

title: Songlin Yang (@SonglinYang4)
summary:
A super long overdue (3+ years?) post on scaling laws.
Compute is expensive. Scaling laws are a way to help us reason about the optimal compute allocation between data and model size before committing to a large run.
The post covers what scaling laws predict, how compute-optimal allocation works, why Kaplan et al. and Chinchilla disagree, and how data limits + fitting details make extrapolation tricky.

linked_urls.title: Scaling Laws, Carefully | Lil'Log
linked_urls.summary: Scaling laws are one of the most critical empirical findings in deep learning. The observation is simple in form: the training loss $L$ decreases predictably as we scale up model size $N$, dataset size $D$, and compute $C$, following a power-law curve, which appears as a straight line on a log-log plot. We can view scaling laws as a framework for describing the relationship between compute, loss, model size and data; at its core, it is about how to allocate precious compute optimally between $N$ and $D$.

The long-context demands of agentic AI accelerated attention research aimed at overcoming the context wall. Over the past year, linear attention has become mainstream, most notably with Gated Delta Networks (GDNs) by @songlinyang4 gaining strong traction among open-weight models. Following the invention of GDN, @Alibaba_Qwen adopted it in Qwen 3.5, while @kimi_moonshot improved upon it with Kimi Delta Attention. On the sparse attention side, @deepseek_ai again led open research with Native Sparse Attention and DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA). Inspired by DSA, @MiniMax_AI developed MiniMax Sparse Attention, and @ZhipuAI advanced it further with IndexShare in GLM-5.2. Finally, the SWA-GQA hybrid attention approach was popularized by @cohere and recently refined by the @xiaomimimo team, which released detailed ablation studies. We thank all the open model training labs for sharing their knowledge, research, and excellent open-weight models. (6/8)

Introducing EdgeBench, a benchmark designed to study how agents learn from environments over at least 12~72-hour runs. We find that performance follows a log-sigmoid function of environment interaction time with high precision.

linked_urls.summary: The concept of recursive self-improvement (RSI) dates back to I. J. Good (1965), where he defined an “ultraintelligent machine” as a system that can surpass humans in all intellectual activities and design better machines to improve itself. Yudkowsky (2008) used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” for a specific feedback loop: an AI uses its current intelligence to improve the cognitive machinery that produces its intelligence. This feedback loop in modern AI may indicate the model rewriting its own weights directly, or more broadly the model improves the training pipeline and the deployment system, which in turn enables a better successor model with improved performance across economically valuable tasks. The speed of research development in AI has been shown to drastically accelerated in frontier labs (Anthropic; OpenAI).

summary:
Some numbers behind the "deeply optimized" part:
1. ShortConv runs 4x per layer across ~66 layers. We fused it everywhere: into the attention prologue (with QK-norm + KV store) and into the all-reduce on the residual stream. The fused all-reduce kernel is 2-3.6x faster than the unfused chain, +5-8% end-to-end.
2. Prefill full CUDA graph captures the entire forward, ShortConv included. No more eager fallbacks bubbling the GPU; +14-17% at launch-bound shapes.
3. MXFP8 KV cache: 2x capacity, quantization fused into the attention prologue, within ~14% of bf16.
Full write-up in the blog ⬇️

Key results:
➤ Inkling debuts at 41 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, making it the leading open weights release from a U.S. lab. Inkling scores 3 points higher on the Intelligence Index (41) than the previous leading U.S. open weights model, Nemotron 3 Ultra (38), and also beats Gemma 4 31B (29) and gpt-oss-120b (24)
➤ Inkling stands out on agentic performance. It scores higher than both Kimi K2.6 and DeepSeek v4 Flash on both GDPval-AA v2 and 𝜏³-Banking: Inkling scores an Elo of 1238 on GDPval-AA v2, higher than Kimi K2.6 (1190) and DeepSeek v4 Flash max (1189) and scores 24% on 𝜏³-Banking, higher than Kimi K2.6 (21%) and just above DeepSeek v4 Flash max (23%)

➤ Inkling natively supports image and audio multimodal inputs, a key differentiator among open weights models. Inkling accepts text, image, and audio input modalities. title: Songlin Yang (@SonglinYang4)
summary:
Incredibly proud of the team. After countless late nights, Inkling is out, and I especially want to highlight the post-training stack and RL recipes behind it.
A few of my favorite details:
We scaled our largest RL run to 30M+ rollouts and thousands of continuous training steps—with no collapse, no restarts, and stable KL and entropy throughout. Reasoning performance improved log-linearly from the SFT initialization all the way to the released checkpoint. A number of innovations under the hood made this possible, and the result is a strong testament to our post-training technology.
We trained controllable thinking effort directly through RL. By varying the system message and per-token cost, the model learned to trade off tokens and performance on demand.
We also saw an emergent shift in reasoning style: as RL progressed, the chain of thought became increasingly compressed, shedding grammatical overhead. Inkling reasons like a caveman mathematician—a distinctive style unlike that of other open-source models.
We’re also previewing Inkling-small today and plan to release it very soon. It is exceptionally capable for its size, and we expect the community will find it broadly useful.
Building a simple, stable, and scalable RL stack in such a short time was something few thought possible. This team proved otherwise.

title: Songlin Yang (@SonglinYang4)
clean_title: Assessing the Kimi K3 pretraining relative to Opus and Mythos models
summary:
I did some quick tests that indicated that the Kimi K3 pretrain is around halfway between Opus 4 and Opus 4.5. So ~10 months behind Anthropic. These tests probably understate data improvements, so overall I think it's a similarly good pretrain to Opus 4.5 (~8 months behind). These tests are better at measuring "general pretrain capability" than at incorporating (coding-specific) data quality.
This was prompted by me thinking more and realizing that my claim that "As a pretrain, it's probably somewhere between 4.8 and Mythos (around halfway between?)" was probably too bullish on the model and that I might as well test and find out. (And yep, this was very wrong.)
I think Mythos is a pretty big step up in pretraining, so K3 might be more than 8 months behind on the historical pretraining trend relative to Mythos (as in, Mythos is >>3 months ahead of K3 and Mythos was fully done training ~5 months ago).
Overall, this makes me suspect more of the improvements are due to distillation-type effects and makes me think the full catch-up times would be somewhat longer (if Ant/OpenAI stopped but investment still followed current trends). Minimally, more of the improvement probably lives in post-training/mid-training.
For reference, the same test indicates K2.6 is around halfway between Sonnet 4 and Sonnet 4.5. (And this roughly corresponds to some other similar measures.)
Sorry about the error.
Quoting @RyanGreenblatt
Kimi K3 was significantly but not massively above my expectations. I'd tentatively guess it's similar in overall usefulness/usability to Opus 4.8 and in overall capability somewhat above Opus 4.8 (while also being somewhat more benchmaxxed). As a pretrain, it's probably somewhere between 4.8 and Mythos (around halfway between?). Maybe this implies Kimi is like 8 or so months behind Anthropic in overall model strength/goodness (including usability) and like 6 or so months behind on overall capability (somewhat below Mythos Preview).
This gap is presumably reduced by distillation (and more generally using OpenAI/Anthropic models) and algorithm leakage/diffusion, so I think that hypothetically if the US completely stopped and recent algos didn't diffuse, it would maybe take Kimi like 10 months to fully catch up to the best internal (including in development) Anthropic model. (I think this notion might be a better measure of where Anthropic/OpenAI are relative to Kimi, even though this hypothetical won't happen.) And if the US completely stopped, it might take Kimi around 27 months to reach the level the US would otherwise have reached one year from now (as in, with a year of further progress).
My views here are pretty sensitive to how much benchmark performance is representative to overall usability.
I think I now expect an open-weight AI which is straightforwardly "Mythos-level at cyber" (including usability etc.) in like 5 months supposing Kimi and others don't change their open-weight model policy. (I don't have a strong view about how big of a deal this is for cyber, but it may cause significant political consequences. This could be a significant overestimate of the time required.)
I wonder what's driving Kimi being closer than I would have expected. Options include:
- Experiment compute is significantly less important than labor (and labor at Kimi is competitive, which seems super plausible)
- Implies more of a speedup from AI automating AI R&D and a bigger software-only intelligence explosion.
- Or possibly Kimi is just doing much better than US companies and this is overcoming experiment compute disadvantages.
- Algorithms are diffusing a lot / quickly (from e.g. OpenAI to Kimi).
- Perf is overstated / benchmaxxed a lot.
- Distillation / using OpenAI or Anthropic frontier AIs in AI development is very helpful for catching up. (But I'd guess Kimi K3 is a competitive pretrain which distillation doesn't help with?)
- US companies aren't going as fast as they could for whatever reason.
clean_summary: Songlin Yang tests the Kimi K3 pretraining model and finds it is roughly halfway between Opus 4 and Opus 4.5 in capability, making it about 8 to 10 months behind Anthropic's models. These tests suggest that much of the recent improvements may come from post-training effects like distillation rather than raw pretraining data, and the actual catch-up time could be longer if current trends continue. The analysis also compares Kimi K3's position to previous models like K2.6 and considers factors such as experiment compute, AI automation, and algorithm diffusion that might influence the model's progress. Overall, the work indicates Kimi's model strength is close to Mythos-level in usability within a few months, with potential political implications depending on how quickly open-weight models advance.

title: Songlin Yang (@SonglinYang4)
clean_title: Can models run deeper at test time than during training and how to optimize for it
summary:
Can a model run deeper at test time than it was ever trained to? And if depth becomes a loop instead of a stack, do we need better optimizers to keep training stable?
@CoreAutoAI is collaborating with @tilderesearch on an optimizer x architecture competition: "One Layer Deeper"
We picked a cursed problem y = x^(2^T) mod N where each squaring depends on the last. A vanilla transformer has a fixed depth so it falls flat on its face the moment T exceeds the serial compute it can do in one forward pass. A fun reminder that architectures have inductive biases.
This isn't quite a nano-gpt speedrun experience and it's not a typical @GPU_MODE kernel competition either, it's closer in spirit to the LLM efficiency competition I worked on many years ago with @weiwei_msr and @Jisaacso in that it's open ended in a specific way.
The UX is kernelbot like, your submission is a single python file that defines your model, optimizer and loss. You don't need a GPU to participate at all since we're reusing a queue based job system powered by @modal and @northflank
There's tons of unexplored ideas and I'm really not sure what will win out but I'd be particularly excited to see people playing with new optimizers, adaptive depth and depth extrapolation.
Since this is a new format, we'll work with the community to refine the rules for another week before we start for real. Submissions are open now!!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HNekGdRbkAAXGM2.jpg
clean_summary: Can a model run deeper at test time than it was trained to? If depth becomes a loop instead of a stack, better optimizers might be needed to keep training stable. @CoreAutoAI and @tilderesearch are collaborating on an 'One Layer Deeper' optimizer x architecture competition, focusing on a challenging problem where each squaring depends on the last. Traditional transformers with fixed depth struggle when T exceeds their serial compute capacity, highlighting how architecture biases influence performance. The competition is open-ended, allowing participants to submit models, optimizers, and losses via a simple Python file, without requiring a GPU, using a queue-based system. The goal is to explore new ideas like adaptive depth and depth extrapolation, with community rules being refined over the next week.

why can the china labs build glm-5.2, kimi k3, and many more to come? it is because of the openness. not just the open weights but the whole ecosystem. most of the work done in the china labs is carried by interns. i met brilliant undergrad and graduate interns who deeply understand the model training details, and they are 100x more open to share. that means the talent that knows how to train llms in china is 100x greater in number than the talent in the us, and it is growing

clean_summary: Why can Chinese labs build models like glm-5.2 and kimi k3? Because of openness, not just in open weights but in the entire ecosystem. Most work in Chinese labs is carried out by interns who deeply understand model training and are eager to share knowledge, indicating that the talent capable of training large language models in China is vastly larger and growing. In contrast, the US AI ecosystem is more closed, with frontier labs not hiring many interns and key techniques kept secret by a small group of privileged researchers. The core issue is open versus closed science; training an LLM is accessible to any average CS student if given the opportunity. Labs should adopt more openness and hire more interns, similar to practices at DeepMind and Facebook in the pre-LLM era.

Ling-3.0 starts with native hybrid-linear attention: KDA and MLA layers stacked 5:1.
KDA gives fine-grained control over long-range memory, while 1/64 expert activation makes MoE compute more efficient.
It supports 256K context natively and can scale to 1M.

title: Songlin Yang (@SonglinYang4)
summary:
Congratulations to the Ling team @AntLingAGI on the release of Ling-3.0-flash! 🎉 A 124B MoE model activating just 5.1B parameters per token—with hybrid-linear attention and native 256K context—is an exciting contribution to production-scale agent systems.
We also applaud the team’s announce-first, open-source-next release approach. Separating the announcement from the weight release lets the model team freeze the final checkpoint, configuration, tokenizer, and serving semantics, while giving open-source inference projects a stable window for correctness testing, performance tuning, Docker builds, and recipe validation. The community also gets a clear timeline instead of an ambiguous “coming soon.”
This is not a step back from day-0 support—it is a more sustainable way to deliver day-0 support for the artifacts users will actually run.
vLLM’s open-source support for Ling-3.0-flash is coming soon and will be available when the model weights are open-sourced. We hope more model vendors adopt this release pattern in the future!
Congrats again—we can’t wait to see what the community builds! 🚀
Quoting @AntLingAGI
Today, we’re releasing Ling-3.0-flash—a hybrid-reasoning MoE model built for production-scale agents.
124B parameters. Just 5.1B active per token.
With 1/8 of the total and 1/12 of the active parameters, it matches or beats our 1T flagship model on most benchmarks shown.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HN7kMd9acAMkWTd.jpg
